statement: By using the substitution $x=\\dfrac{\\pi}{2}-t$, or otherwise, evaluate $I=\\int_{0}^{\\pi/2}\\dfrac{\\sin x}{\\sin x+\\cos x}\,dx$.
solution: Let $I=\\int_{0}^{\\pi/2}\\frac{\\sin x}{\\sin x+\\cos x}\,dx$. Under $x=\\pi/2-t$ we have $dx=-dt$ and the limits swap, giving $I=\\int_{0}^{\\pi/2}\\frac{\\cos t}{\\cos t+\\sin t}\,dt$. Adding the two expressions for $I$, $2I=\\int_{0}^{\\pi/2}\\frac{\\sin x+\\cos x}{\\sin x+\\cos x}\,dx=\\int_{0}^{\\pi/2}1\,dx=\\frac{\\pi}{2}$. Therefore $I=\\pi/4$.
hints: Apply the substitution x=pi/2 - t to get a second form of I.
Add the original and substituted integrals.
The numerators then combine to sin x + cos x.
